children: By Elizabeth Bernstein
I've received hundreds of letters recently from readers who aren't speaking to a family member. Many are desperate to heal the rift, but have no idea how. "What can I possibly do?" they plead.

Many experts believe that there is an estrangement crisis happening across America. Prominent research — published in Cornell sociologist Karl Pillemer's 2020 book, "Fault Lines: Fractured Families and How to Mend Them" — shows that a quarter of the population is estranged from, or has cut ties with, a close relative at any given time. About 10% are estranged from a parent or child.

On social media, the picture looks even more dire. Since the beginning of the pandemic in 2020, the number of new videos posted on TikTok that mentioned cutting off or going low contact with parents increased more than 10-fold, according to Infegy, which analyzes social conversations and trends.

Yet very little evidence-based advice exists on how to repair an estrangement. Most therapists receive no formal training on this problem. In fact, many are coming to the issue only recently, after witnessing widespread demand for help.
Even experienced family therapists say the problem can be intractable, as it's extraordinarily difficult to get both sides together to talk and listen.

Cornell's Pillemer, who has been studying family conflict for four decades, has some answers. He's conducted hundreds of in-depth interviews with families that had an estrangement, including 100 who went on to reconcile. The average estrangement lasts four years, according to his research, and the damage can spread to the entire family. Older adults often name it as one of their biggest regrets, Pillemer found.
Those who reconcile, even the ones who initiated the estrangement, describe that a burden was lifted, his research shows.

Should everyone attempt repair? Not necessarily. Estrangement is sometimes necessary, especially in cases of ongoing emotional or physical abuse. But most family rifts fall into gray areas, Pillemer says — the result of more run-of-the-mill relationship problems, such as arguments over in-laws, lifestyle or politics.

"In most rifts, the costs to you and your family outweigh the grievance," he says. An estrangement can lead to chronic stress, research shows, even for the person who initiated it. The fallout often affects the whole family, including innocent bystanders like siblings or grandchildren. And estranged people lose the safety net families typically provide.
"A reconciliation — even a limited one with clear boundaries — is usually the better choice for your own sake," Pillemer says.
Through his research, he has identified four main strategies that helped people successfully repair an estrangement:
Let go of the past. Family members who reconciled accepted that their accounts of the past wouldn't align — and focused on building a future rather than litigating history.

They almost always gave up on an admission of guilt. "They realized that an apology on demand was not going to be much of an apology," Pillemer says. Meaningful ones come later, after reconciliation, once each side understands its part in the rift.

Examine your own role. Someone who experiences rejection tends to shut down or attack back. "They become so defensive that they can't see the other person's viewpoint," Pillemer says. He calls this "defensive ignorance."

Those who reconciled stopped blaming each other and came to understand the rift as a relationship problem, not just the fault of the other person. "Believing that it is the other person's fault limits your actions," Pillemer says. "Understanding some of the role you played allows you to do something different."

Change expectations. We'd all like ideal relationships, but that's not always possible. Not everyone has the capacity to show up the way we need. Those who decided to expect less from the other person were able to reconcile without constant disappointment.
"You can accept someone's limitations without excusing them," Pillemer says. "People found this liberating."

Set clear terms for engagement. Be specific. For example, don't say: "You have to respect my boundaries." Instead, try: "You cannot show up at my house unannounced. If you do, I cannot continue this relationship."

For many, the process of reconciliation can fuel personal growth because it teaches them about themselves, Pillemer says. "And even if it doesn't work out, you will feel a lot less guilty because you tried."
For Julie Kreutzer, 65, repairing her estrangement with her mother took years.

Kreutzer's parents divorced when she was five and afterward her mother told her that her father remarried and lost interest in seeing her. Then, when Kreutzer was in her 30s, she heard from an aunt who explained that her father never wanted the separation; it was her mother who had enforced it.

Kreutzer told her mother that she was devastated. Unsatisfied with her mother's response, Kreutzer didn't speak with her for two years. Then her father, with whom Kreutzer had reconnected, encouraged her to repair the rift, reminding her that you only have two parents and life is short.
So Kreutzer sent her mother a card. The response was lukewarm, she says. For the next few years, she saw her mom occasionally but only if Kreutzer made the effort to make it happen, she says.

Then Kreutzer thought about her son. And she realized that you can do the best for your child and still make mistakes. She decided to accept her mom for who she is and focus on her positive qualities, such as her sense of humor. And she set a term for reconciliation: Her mother needs to be honest with her going forward.
She also tried to understand why her mom did what she did. "I let go of the past," Kreutzer says. "I realized that no one is perfect, so we need to pick ourselves up and move on."
Now she often visits her mom, who is 89 and was diagnosed with Alzheimer's last year.
"To take a dead relationship and bring it back to life is an amazing thing," she says.
